before.body_md:
# Interview Strategy by Role

## Why This Matters
Career growth is a compound system. Better decisions early reduce switching costs and improve long-term optionality.

## Practical Framework
1. Define one 12-month target role with explicit success criteria.
2. Build a capability backlog across knowledge, projects, and collaboration behavior.
3. Run 4-week execution sprints and collect measurable evidence.
4. Review outcomes quarterly and adjust strategy using market and fit signals.

## Implementation Checklist
- Clear role target and industry context
- Evidence-based skill gap map
- Portfolio or project proof
- Feedback loop with mentors and stakeholders

snapshot.title: Interview Strategy by Role
snapshot.excerpt: Prepare interview evidence around the work a vacancy requires, with role-specific practice, a worked answer and ways to handle missing experience.
snapshot.body_md:
# Interview Strategy by Role

Prepare for the work in the vacancy, then choose examples that make your own contribution understandable. A polished general introduction cannot answer every employer's question about technical judgment, customer decisions or managing people.

Start with the current job description, your submitted application and the interview invitation. The steps below are a preparation method, not a way to predict the questions or guarantee an offer.

## Turn the vacancy into questions you can answer

Highlight the responsibilities and requirements separately. For each important responsibility, write an ordinary-language task, the evidence you can discuss and what you still need to ask. Preserve words such as “required” and “desirable”; do not silently upgrade or remove a condition.

| Vacancy wording | Task to understand | Evidence to prepare | Question still open |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinate delivery across teams | Notice a dependency, agree an owner and follow up | A real example of handling an overdue handover | Who decides when priorities conflict? |
| Analyse service information | Check inputs and explain a recommendation | An analysis with assumptions, checks and limits | What data and decisions does this team own? |
| Resolve customer problems | Understand the issue and work within service rules | A case showing your action, authority and escalation | What can this role decide without approval? |
| Supervise colleagues | Set expectations and respond to a difficulty | Your actual responsibility and what happened | Does this role include formal people management? |

These are invented vacancy fragments. Your employer may use different tasks and standards. If a requirement is unclear, record a question instead of pretending the title explains it.

## Change the practice task to match the work

Job titles are starting points. Use the responsibilities to decide which part of an example needs the most explanation.

| Work being assessed | What to make visible in practice | A useful follow-up question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical or analytical work | Assumptions, method, checks and uncertainty | What would change your conclusion? |
| Customer-facing work | The person's problem, available options and your authority | When would you escalate rather than promise a solution? |
| Project or operations support | Dependencies, owners, records and follow-through | What would you do if an owner did not respond? |
| People management | Expectations, feedback, support and decisions you actually owned | How did you distinguish a skill gap from an unclear expectation? |

These are editorial prompts, not universal hiring criteria. For a past-experience question, use an actual episode. For a hypothetical exercise, make clear that you are explaining a proposed approach rather than reporting something you have done.

## Match preparation to the actual interview format

Ask the recruiter about the format, duration, participants and any task or presentation instructions. Check whether materials, software or advance preparation are expected. Discuss access needs through the employer's process where relevant; local requirements differ.

For a past-experience question, explain the situation, your responsibility, your action, the result and what you learned. For a technical exercise, practise explaining assumptions, checks and an uncertainty rather than memorising only an answer. For a case discussion, clarify the objective and constraints before recommending a solution. For a management conversation, distinguish your decisions from a colleague's work and explain how you supported or corrected the process.

The advertised format takes priority over these examples. Do not assume every technical role uses a coding task or every manager is assessed through the same exercise.

## Worked example: one real project, different relevant evidence

This is a fictional teaching example. The project, invitation and feedback are invented; there was no interview or hiring outcome.

Ravi helped organise a community event. Two suppliers had different delivery dates, and the team had not recorded who would confirm them. Ravi made a shared list of dates and owners, checked it with the organiser and contacted the two suppliers with permission. Both confirmations arrived before the event. Ravi did not manage the budget or supervise the volunteers.

Ravi is preparing for an invented project-support vacancy that asks for coordination and accurate records. His first practice answer is: “I led a successful event and improved communication.” It hides the evidence and overstates his role.

A better answer is: “Our event team had two unconfirmed deliveries. I was responsible for tracking them, not the whole event. I listed the dates and contact owners, checked the list with the organiser, and followed up with the suppliers. Both deliveries were confirmed before the event. I kept the confirmation notes, but we did not measure whether my list saved time. Next time I would agree the owner when each supplier is booked.”

For an analytical vacancy, the same story does not establish analysis skills. Ravi would need another genuine example involving checking information and drawing a supported conclusion. For a supervisor vacancy, coordinating suppliers does not establish that he managed employees. He can explain that limit and discuss relevant experience without inventing authority.

Ravi asks a practice partner to identify his responsibility, action and evidence from the answer. The partner asks: “What happened when a supplier did not respond?”

In this invented account, Ravi checks his notes and adds: “One supplier missed the reply date. I checked that I had used the agreed contact, then told the organiser that confirmation was still missing. The organiser approved a phone follow-up. I made the call and recorded the confirmed date. I did not change the order or promise a new delivery arrangement myself.”

That answer makes the escalation and his limits visible. It gives the practice partner something specific to question. In this fictional exercise, the next step is clearer evidence, not a more impressive job title.

## Practise questions that expose gaps

Choose one important responsibility and say your answer aloud. Ask yourself or a practice partner:

- What did I personally decide or do?
- What alternatives did I consider, and why did I choose this action?
- What can I verify about the outcome? What remains unknown?
- What would I change if the same problem happened again?

Use confidential work only in a form you are allowed to discuss. Removing names alone may not make restricted material shareable. Use a permitted general account or a clearly labelled hypothetical example when necessary; do not upload employer documents to practise. If you lack an example, say what experience you do have and how you would approach a hypothetical task. Label hypothetical reasoning clearly.

Do not replace task evidence with a personality label or an IQ/EQ score. Those do not demonstrate that you meet this vacancy's requirements.

## Prepare questions that help you choose, too

Ask about the first priorities, the standard of an acceptable deliverable, who reviews it and what support is available. Pay, hours and working conditions can also be important decision questions; asking about them is not evidence of poor motivation.

Before the interview, check the location or video link, required materials and a contact for technical problems. If instructions are missing, ask for clarification. If a task requests confidential information or work you cannot safely provide, explain the constraint and ask about an appropriate alternative.

Afterwards, record the actual questions, where your evidence was clear and what you could not answer. A rejection or silence alone does not identify the cause. Use specific feedback where available and revise the relevant example or target requirement.

Your next action is to complete one responsibility-to-evidence row and practise its follow-up questions. If the missing evidence is an artifact, use the [career-switch portfolio guide](/en/career/guides/build-portfolio-for-career-switch). When an offer arrives, move to the [salary negotiation framework](/en/career/guides/salary-negotiation-framework), or return to the [career planning hub](/en/career/guides) if the target itself remains unclear.

## Sources and scope

- [National Careers Service: Interview tips](https://nationalcareers.service.gov.uk/careers-advice/interview-advice/), read 22 October 2026. England's public careers service recommends checking the format, researching the employer and preparing relevant experience.
- [National Careers Service: The STAR method](https://nationalcareers.service.gov.uk/careers-advice/interview-advice/the-star-method), read 22 October 2026. A structure for describing experience, not a prediction of interview success.

The table, practice questions and Ravi's example are editorial teaching tools. Employer criteria and local accessibility or employment rules need their own current sources.

snapshot.title: Salary Negotiation Framework
snapshot.excerpt: Compare an offer's recurring pay, conditional rewards and practical terms, then prepare a focused request and a decision if the employer declines.
snapshot.body_md:
# Salary Negotiation Framework

Prepare a request you can explain, compare the whole offer and decide what you will do if the answer is no. No universal percentage increase or confident script can establish the right salary for a particular role.

This guide concerns preparing a job-offer conversation. For an internal pay review, first check your employer's review timetable, criteria and decision maker. The same evidence record can help, but an external-offer process is not automatically your employer's process.

## Establish what is actually offered

Ask for the role, location, hours, pay components, conditions and response deadline in writing. Clarify whether an amount is annual or monthly, its currency, and whether it is gross or take-home pay. Do not compare a contractor's revenue with an employee's salary as if the costs and protections were identical.

Separate guaranteed pay from conditional components. A target bonus, possible future raise or unvested equity is not cash you can rely on for ordinary bills. Ask for the relevant terms rather than inserting an optimistic value. Check unfamiliar tax, visa, contract or repayment conditions with a qualified local source before committing.

| Component | Written offer | What remains to verify | Priority for me |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base pay | Amount, currency and pay period | Hours and any conditions | Fill in |
| Variable compensation | Eligibility and stated terms | How it is determined and when payable | Fill in |
| Leave and work arrangement | Written policy or offer provision | Approval conditions and actual role constraints | Fill in |
| One-off support | Amount and purpose | Timing and repayment terms | Fill in |
| Decision deadline | Date and time | Whether more time is possible | Fill in |

## Build a relevant comparison, not a borrowed number

Record current vacancies or credible pay information for similar responsibilities, level, location and employment arrangement. Note the source and date. A broad advertised range may cover several levels; a national occupational average may combine very different employers. Neither tells you where this offer must sit.

Then list the experience you can substantiate against this role. Explain the relevant task and evidence rather than claiming you will create a financial return you have not measured. Do not invent another offer or describe an interview as a secured alternative.

Keep your minimum workable conditions private in your own decision record. Include realistic living costs and commitments, but distinguish those personal needs from an employer-facing explanation of the requested package. For your own budget, compare expected take-home pay with costs; do not treat gross salary as spendable income. If the evidence is too weak for a number, ask about the budgeted range and how placement within it is decided.

## Make a focused, conditional request

Before accepting, ask whether the component you care about is flexible. State your interest, the specific request and its basis. For example:

“Thank you for the offer. I am interested in the role. Given the responsibility for X and my documented experience doing Y, is there flexibility in the base pay? I would like to discuss [amount and currency], based on [dated, comparable evidence].”

Fill the brackets with genuine evidence. This wording is a conversation aid, not a guarantee that negotiation is available or risk-free. Some roles have fixed bands or programme-wide terms.

If pay is fixed, ask about a different condition that matters to you and can actually be changed. A future review date is useful to understand, but a review is not a promised increase. Avoid trading away a requirement you cannot afford to lose merely to reach an agreement.

## Worked example: compare certainty before counting the total

This is a fictional teaching example. All amounts are invented accounting units, not salaries, currency benchmarks or market recommendations. There was no employer negotiation or measured result.

For the arithmetic only, assume a complete paid year under an unchanged work arrangement. All figures below are gross amounts before deductions. Elena has set an illustrative comparison threshold of 50,000 recurring gross units per year. This threshold is an assumption, not a calculation of her living costs or take-home pay.

The invented offer contains 48,000 base units per year and a possible 4,000 bonus. Elena initially writes “total 52,000, acceptable.” That treats a conditional amount as certain.

| Illustrative component | First complete year | Following complete year, if terms stay unchanged |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base pay | 48,000 gross units | 48,000 gross units |
| Possible bonus | 4,000 if its conditions are met | Not guaranteed |
| One-off payment proposed later | 2,000, only if confirmed and payable under its terms | No repeat payment |
| Base plus proposed one-off payment | 50,000 before deductions, if both are payable in that year | 48,000 before deductions |

She records the base as 48,000 and the bonus as conditional. She asks how the bonus works and researches current, comparable local role information before deciding on a requested amount. Her transferable evidence is a documented example of coordinating the same kind of delivery, not a claimed revenue gain.

In the invented conversation, the employer says the base is fixed and proposes the 2,000 one-off payment. Elena checks when it would be paid and whether it could have to be repaid. Even if it is payable in full, it does not bring recurring gross pay to her illustrative 50,000 threshold. She asks about hours and whether any relevant recurring component can change, then compares the written answer with her minimum conditions. A real decision would also require a separate check of deductions, payment timing and actual costs.

If there is no workable recurring arrangement, she can decline or continue her search if her circumstances permit. If she chooses to accept for another reason, she records the unresolved trade-off instead of calling the package financially equivalent. The example teaches a comparison; it does not decide for a real applicant.

## Respond to a refusal or a changed offer

- **Fixed terms:** confirm what is fixed, then evaluate the actual package. Repeating the same request without new information does not create a budget.
- **Insufficient decision time:** ask for the time you need and explain what you must clarify. The employer may refuse; decide using the real deadline.
- **Changed responsibilities or location:** rebuild the comparison. Earlier pay evidence may no longer describe the role.
- **Unclear conditions:** ask for written clarification before relying on them. Seek appropriate local advice for significant contractual uncertainty.

Once the conversation is complete, check that the written terms match what was agreed, including any conditions and response deadline. Do not treat a friendly verbal possibility as an approved benefit.

Your next action is to complete the offer table and identify the one unresolved condition that could change your decision. Use the [career risk guide](/en/career/guides/career-risk-management) to make a feasible fallback, or the [interview guide](/en/career/guides/interview-strategy-by-role) if you are still gathering role evidence.

## Source and limits

[Harvard Mignone Center for Career Success: Evaluating and Negotiating Job and Internship Offers](https://careerservices.fas.harvard.edu/resources/harvard-college-evaluating-and-negotiating-job-and-internship-offers/), read 22 October 2026, provides U.S. university career guidance on written offers, compensation components and negotiation before commitment. Its student and U.S. context is not a statement of worldwide employment law or a salary benchmark. The comparison table and fictional calculation above are original editorial aids, not personalised financial or legal advice.

snapshot.title: Networking That Actually Works
snapshot.excerpt: Use informational conversations to answer a career question, approach people respectfully and turn what you learn into a concrete next step.
snapshot.body_md:
# Networking That Actually Works

Choose something you need to learn, approach a relevant person with a manageable question and use the answer to improve a decision. A useful professional conversation does not need to produce a referral to count as useful.

If you are exploring a career, an informational conversation is different from a job interview. You are asking about the work and its context; the other person is not agreeing to assess you, find vacancies or advocate for you.

## Begin with an information gap

Write a question that would change your next action. “How do I succeed?” is difficult to answer. “When your team receives conflicting requests, who decides which one takes priority?” gives the person a concrete part of work to explain.

Check what is already public before contacting someone. Read the relevant role description, employer information or project notes. This lets you ask about a remaining uncertainty rather than request a summary of an entire profession.

| Decision I face | What I can read first | Question for someone with relevant experience | How I will use the answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether to investigate a new field | Current role descriptions | What occupies a normal week, including routine work? | Choose a realistic introductory task |
| Whether my experience transfers | Target responsibilities | What evidence helps you judge this particular task? | Improve a sample or identify a gap |
| Whether a role's arrangement fits | Published hours and location | What does the stated arrangement look like in this team? | Verify a constraint with the employer |

These are prompts. One person's account describes their circumstances and may not represent another employer, region or level.

## Make an invitation easy to understand and decline

Choose a person whose actual work relates to your question. A colleague, alumni contact, professional group or public event may offer a suitable route. Follow the community's contact rules; access to someone's profile is not permission to send repeated messages.

A short invitation can contain your context, what you have read, one question and a bounded request:

“I work in customer support and am exploring service operations. Your public talk about request handovers raised a question about who owns exceptions. Would you be willing to discuss that for 15 minutes? I am looking to understand the work; there is no problem if you are unavailable.”

This is an invented example, not a message already sent. Choose a duration you can honour and use an appropriate channel. Do not attach confidential work, disclose someone else's contact details or imply a shared relationship that does not exist.

## Have a conversation, then check the interpretation

Briefly explain why the question matters, then listen. Ask for a concrete example that the person is allowed to discuss. Separate an observed practice from their opinion about what should happen. If a word or process is unfamiliar, ask what it means in that setting.

Respect the agreed time. Ask permission before recording, quoting or introducing the person to someone else. They can decline follow-up contact. A conversation is not an endorsement you can add to a public profile.

## Worked example: useful learning without a referral

This is a fictional teaching example. The people, messages and answers are invented; no practitioner was interviewed and no job outcome was observed.

Leila is considering a move from retail coordination into warehouse operations. She has read target vacancies but does not understand how teams handle late supplier information. Her first draft message says, “Can you refer me to operations jobs?” She has not identified a vacancy or established that the person can refer her.

She changes the request to a short conversation about handovers. In the imagined response, a practitioner explains that their own team uses a named owner for each exception and escalates missing information at a scheduled review. Leila writes “one team's practice” in her notes. She does not conclude that every warehouse uses this process or that she now understands the sector.

Her action is to build a synthetic handover log containing an owner, open question and escalation point, then compare it with actual target requirements. She asks which public resources explain the terminology. The person declines to review a sample because of time limits, so Leila uses the public resources and seeks another appropriate feedback route. She does not keep asking for a review or treat the refusal as criticism of her ability.

Her thank-you note identifies the useful distinction: “I had confused tracking a request with owning the exception. I am checking the target team's responsibilities before claiming that experience.” No referral occurs. The conversation still resolves a real question and changes her preparation.

## Keep a record that leads to action

Copy these fields into private notes: date; context and region; question; what the person actually said; your interpretation; what remains unknown; next check; and any permission for further contact. Avoid collecting unnecessary personal information.

Afterwards, thank them and, if welcome, report how you used the information. Share something relevant when you have it; reciprocity need not be immediate or transactional. Do not promise introductions, work or access you cannot provide.

If there is no response, use public information or another suitable route. One polite follow-up after a reasonable interval can be an editorial option where the channel permits it; it is not a required sequence. Stop when someone declines or a community asks you not to contact members. Silence does not tell you why a person is unavailable.

If several conversations disagree, compare their employer, seniority, location and task conditions. Keep the disagreement visible and verify the decisive requirement with the organisation or official authority that owns it.

Your next action is to write one decision question and find the public information that already answers part of it. Use the [cross-industry guide](/en/career/guides/cross-industry-move-strategy) to organise transfer questions, or the [professional brand guide](/en/career/guides/personal-brand-for-professionals) to make your own evidence clearer. The [career planning hub](/en/career/guides) connects these steps to a broader plan.

## Source and scope

[UC Berkeley Career Engagement: Informational Interviews](https://www.career.berkeley.edu/start-exploring/informational-interviews/), read 22 October 2026, distinguishes exploration conversations from job interviews and recommends preparation, respecting time and recording follow-up actions. Its alumni services are specific to Berkeley; this guide does not imply that readers can access them. The invitation, table and fictional example are editorial aids, with no promised response, referral or employment outcome.

snapshot.title: Personal Brand for Professionals
snapshot.excerpt: Make your professional claims easier to evaluate through permitted examples, clear attribution and a consistent account of what you have done and are learning.
snapshot.body_md:
# Personal Brand for Professionals

Help a relevant reader understand what work you can do, what evidence supports that claim and how to discuss an appropriate opportunity. You do not need a large audience or a dramatic title to make your experience easier to evaluate.

Begin with an audience and a real task: an employer comparing applicants, a colleague seeking a project contributor or a prospective client checking your experience. Their questions may differ. “Build my brand” is too broad to decide what to publish next.

## Write a claim you can support today

Draft one sentence about the problem you help with, your actual contribution and the setting where you have evidence. “I document service handovers and clarify open requests for small operations teams” is more testable than “I transform businesses.” Use a narrower claim if your experience is a student project or a synthetic sample.

This is not a permanent identity. Keep “I have done,” “I am learning” and “I want to do” separate. Do not describe a certificate as a licence or a collaborative result as your individual achievement.

| Claim I want to make | Evidence a reader can inspect | My actual contribution | Limit or permission to state |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I can clarify a process | A permitted process map and explanation | What I mapped, checked and revised | Not evidence of implementing it |
| I can explain a technical topic | A short explanation for a defined audience | Research, example and revision I produced | Topic and audience are bounded |
| I am learning a new field | A labelled practice artifact | What I attempted and how I checked it | No client, employer approval or production outcome |

The rows are examples, not credentials. Choose evidence appropriate to the reader's actual decision.

## Build a small evidence page before adding more channels

Choose one or two permitted examples that support your claim. For each, state the problem, constraints, your role, work produced, checks and result. Distinguish an implemented result from a proposal or a practice exercise. If you did not measure an impact, say so rather than inventing a percentage.

Use work only when you have permission to share it. Removing a name may not remove confidential information or other people's rights. If permission is uncertain, describe the experience at an appropriate general level or create a fresh synthetic exercise and label it. Do not publish a client's private data, a colleague's contact information or an employer's internal material to make a profile look persuasive.

For deeper artifact design, use the [career-switch portfolio guide](/en/career/guides/build-portfolio-for-career-switch). This page focuses on presenting your current claim consistently; the portfolio guide focuses on building and checking the underlying evidence.

## Worked example: remove a stronger claim that the evidence cannot carry

This is a fictional teaching example. Amina, the documents and the reader response are invented. No audience study or career outcome took place.

Amina has helped record changes for two internal projects. Her public draft says “Operations strategist delivering measurable transformation.” She has no permission to show the project records and no measured transformation result. The wording makes the evidence problem larger.

She creates a separate fictional request log with five invented requests, named placeholder owners and two unresolved dependencies. Her sample explains how she identified missing owners and what she would ask before a handover. It is labelled “synthetic practice example; not client work.” She does not claim that the sample proves she can run a production operation.

Her revised profile says: “I have supported project change tracking and am developing service-handover documentation skills. This synthetic example shows how I record owners, dependencies and open questions.” The linked page explains the difference between her actual experience and the new exercise.

She asks a trusted reader to state, in their own words, what she has done and what the sample demonstrates. In this imagined feedback, the reader thinks she implemented the sample at work. Amina moves the synthetic label next to the title and removes a misleading past-tense sentence. The next review checks that specific misunderstanding. She does not add more posts to compensate for an unclear claim.

If she later gains permission to discuss a genuine project, she can add a separate case with the appropriate limits. The practice example does not become real client work merely because her skills improve.

## Check consistency where a reader will actually look

Compare your CV, profile headline, short introduction and evidence page. They need not use identical wording, but dates, responsibilities, credentials and claims should agree. Make the relevant example easy to find and check that its link works without the reader needing permissions you did not intend.

For a conversation, adapt the introduction to the purpose. A short account of your background, relevant interest and what you hope to learn can be enough; do not recite every role or memorise a promotional speech.

Choose a sustainable way to keep the material current. Update it when an important claim or example changes. Posting frequently is optional and cannot substitute for developing the work itself. A private, permitted example shared with the right reader may serve your task better than a public content schedule.

## Use feedback to decide what to change

- **Readers misunderstand your role:** clarify attribution and remove broad claims before seeking more visibility.
- **Readers understand, but the evidence is weak:** develop or check the artifact; changing the headline will not supply missing experience.
- **The wrong enquiries arrive:** inspect the audience, wording and examples before assuming you need more reach.
- **Sharing would breach a restriction:** stop publication of that material and use a permitted alternative.
- **Your target changes:** revise the claim and example selection. Keep history truthful rather than recasting old work as a different occupation.

Track evidence that answers your purpose: whether a reader understands your contribution, asks a relevant question or can inspect the appropriate work. Views and follower counts alone do not establish trust, competence or better opportunities.

Your next action is to audit one claim against one artifact, then ask a suitable reader what they believe it demonstrates. Use the [networking guide](/en/career/guides/networking-that-actually-works) for a respectful conversation, or the [workplace skill guide](/en/career/guides/improve-workplace-competitiveness) if the next step is stronger evidence rather than presentation.

## Source and limits

[Yale Office of Career Strategy: Tell Me About Yourself](https://ocs.yale.edu/channels/tell-me-about-yourself/), read 22 October 2026, offers guidance on selecting relevant background and practising a natural introduction. Its student prompts are not universal requirements. The claim audit, synthetic case and feedback method above are editorial tools, not validated predictions of reputation, income or hiring.
